reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO nutrition guidance
clinicalPearls: Iodine deficiency is the leading preventable cause of goitre and of acquired intellectual disability worldwide
It occurs in regions with iodine-poor soil and water, historically including large parts of the Himalayan and sub-Himalayan belt of India, and salt iodisation is the mainstay of control
Deficiency in pregnancy is the most serious consequence, causing impaired fetal brain development and, in severe cases, endemic cretinism
The clinical spectrum ranges from diffuse or nodular goitre to hypothyroidism, growth and developmental delay, and neurological deficits
The population iodine status is assessed by median urinary iodine concentration rather than by individual blood tests
Rapid correction of longstanding deficiency, or excess iodine, can occasionally provoke thyroid dysfunction, so replacement is at physiological population levels
Neurological damage sustained in fetal life and infancy is largely irreversible, making prevention through adequate maternal intake essential
reference.pathophysiology: Iodine is an essential substrate for the synthesis of the thyroid hormones thyroxine and triiodothyronine. When dietary intake is inadequate, reduced hormone production lowers feedback inhibition and raises thyroid-stimulating hormone, driving thyroid hyperplasia and goitre as a compensatory response; over time nodularity and, if compensation fails, hypothyroidism develop. Thyroid hormone is critical for normal neuronal migration and myelination in the developing brain, so maternal and early-life deficiency impairs neurodevelopment irreversibly, producing the cognitive and neurological features of iodine deficiency disorders, including cretinism in severe endemic areas.
additionalDifferentials: Sporadic non-toxic goitre and thyroid nodules
Congenital hypothyroidism from thyroid dysgenesis or dyshormonogenesis
additionalInvestigations: Thyroid function tests including TSH and free thyroid hormones
Urinary iodine concentration for assessing population and individual status
Thyroid ultrasound to characterise goitre or nodules
Developmental and neurological assessment in affected children
redFlags: Deficiency in pregnancy threatening fetal neurodevelopment
Large goitre causing airway or oesophageal compression
Overt hypothyroidism, especially in infants where it threatens development
Signs of endemic cretinism requiring urgent public health and clinical action
reference.prognosis: Goitre and hypothyroidism from deficiency can improve with adequate iodine intake, but neurodevelopmental damage from fetal and early-life deficiency is largely permanent, underscoring prevention.
pitfalls: Relying on individual blood iodine levels rather than urinary iodine for status assessment
Overlooking maternal iodine adequacy in pregnancy
Assuming a goitre is always autoimmune and missing endemic iodine deficiency
Causing iodine-induced thyroid dysfunction through excessive supplementation
